result:
The old lighthouse stood on a black cliff, counting storms like a patient keeper of minutes. Its lamp turned through fog and salt, painting the sea with a slow golden blade. Fishermen below trusted that beam more than prayers, because it arrived every night without argument.

Inside, the keeper climbed the spiral stairs with a tin cup of tea warming his hands. He was not lonely, though people in town imagined him so. He had the voices of waves, the diary of weather, and the quiet company of routine. Each evening he polished the glass until it held the moon in pieces. Each morning he recorded wind, visibility, and the names of passing ships.

One night, a letter arrived by supply boat. It was from a child asking whether lighthouses ever felt afraid of the dark. The keeper laughed until he coughed, then wrote back carefully. He said a lighthouse is not brave because it has no fear; it is useful because it has a purpose. Darkness, he explained, is only the place where light has not yet been allowed to enter.

He folded the page and sealed it with wax, feeling oddly younger. When dusk returned, he lit the lamp as always. But that night the beam seemed less like a warning and more like an answer. Far away, a child held the letter under a blanket and smiled. The sea continued its ancient breathing, and the lighthouse kept turning, steady and unafraid. It remembered every storm kindly, always.
